items.prompt: What does a formal org chart show?
choices: Whose advice the boss quietly trusts most
Who reports to whom in the company
Which coworkers enjoy each other's company
items.explanation: The formal chart records reporting lines. It says nothing about trust.

items.prompt: The class list says the class rep picks the lunch spot. Whose view would the informal network point to?
choices: The teacher who wrote out the official class list
The student who sits nearest to the door
The classmate whose opinion the rep checks first
items.explanation: The informal network follows whose judgment the decider actually weighs, not who is on the list.

items.prompt: The informal decision network is mostly...
choices: Unwritten and learned by watching decisions
Printed in the staff handbook and updated yearly
Stored in payroll next to job titles
items.explanation: It is rarely documented anywhere. You learn it by observing how decisions happen.

items.prompt: Which statement about an accurate formal chart is true?
choices: It shows who shapes decisions whenever it is accurate
It can be correct and still miss who shapes decisions
It is wrong whenever an informal network exists
items.explanation: An accurate chart still only answers a reporting-line question.

items.prompt: How can you find the informal network?
choices: Read each person's job title and reporting line closely
Count how many reports each person has
Watch who is consulted before decisions are made
items.explanation: Influence shows up in consultation patterns, not in titles or headcount.

items.prompt: Two charts exist side by side in one organization. Which fits?
choices: Both are real and answer different questions
Only the informal one is real in a company
Only the formal one is real, the rest is gossip
items.explanation: They coexist. Each answers a different question.

items.prompt: A proposal sent through the official chain stalls for weeks. What might that tell you?
choices: The proposal must be bad if nobody replied
The formal route may not be where it gets judged
The official chain is broken and should now be ignored
items.explanation: A stall is not a verdict. The real evaluation may happen somewhere the chart does not show.

items.prompt: Which question does the informal network answer?
choices: Who has to approve my request for time off?
Who writes the review of my yearly performance?
Whose judgment does the decider check first?
items.explanation: Approvals and reviews follow reporting lines. Consultation follows trust.

items.prompt: Maya sends a proposal up the chain, manager to director, and it sits for weeks. Her colleague talks briefly with an untitled teammate from another team, and approval comes within days. Which explanation fits best?
choices: The director ignores written proposals, so only spoken and in-person ideas count here
The teammate holds a hidden title that outranks the director in practice
The director weighs that teammate's judgment first, which no reporting line records
Maya's proposal was weaker, which a stall always proves
items.explanation: The stall is not a verdict on the proposal. The untitled teammate was on the director's real consultation path, which no reporting line records. The other options invent rules nothing in the case supports.
items.reference:
Two charts, two questions
formal: who reports to whom
informal: whose judgment is checked first
both are real, at the same time
Why: only one of them is where a given decision actually gets evaluated.
items.learnMore:
Reporting lines are not trust lines

The formal chart answers who approves what and who writes whose review. The informal network answers whose opinion a decision-maker weighs before deciding. Neither is the fake one.

Common mistake

Assuming the formal chart is the operative one for every kind of decision.
items.reflection: Think of a group you belong to. Who does the official decider quietly check with before choosing, and does that person appear on any chart?

items.prompt: Which statement contrasts the two charts correctly?
choices: Formal position records who is trusted; informal weight records who must sign off
Formal position comes from a title; informal weight builds through repeated trust in someone's judgment
Formal lines change weekly with gossip; informal weight changes only at annual reviews
Formal lines cover small decisions; informal weight covers only decisions above a budget
items.explanation: Formal position is assigned and documented. Informal weight is built from repeated, observed judgment. The distractors swap or distort the two definitions.

items.prompt: Tom's team lead approves his vacation and writes his review. Which chart explains that relationship?
choices: The formal chart, because approvals and reviews follow reporting lines
The informal network, because it records whoever Tom trusts most
Both equally, since the two charts always match exactly
Neither chart, since approvals are decided afresh by each separate request
items.explanation: Vacation approval and reviews are reporting-line functions, so the formal chart explains them. Treating the two charts as always identical, or approvals as random, misses that each chart answers a different question.

items.prompt: A reorg moves several teams under new managers in a single week. What happens to the informal network?
choices: It is redrawn the same day, since trust follows new titles instantly
It disappears until HR publishes an updated influence document
It becomes identical to the new chart, since both are built from the same reporting lines
It shifts more slowly, since trust formed earlier does not follow the new lines
items.explanation: Trust formed through past decisions does not move just because titles did. The informal network adjusts gradually as new working relationships build, so it lags the formal redraw.

items.prompt: Can someone with no direct reports hold real influence?
choices: Yes, if decision-makers trust their judgment
No, influence comes only from having reports
Only when they also hold a director title
items.explanation: Influence comes from trust in judgment, not from headcount.

items.prompt: Where does informal influence usually come from?
choices: A line added to the formal org chart
Years of dependably good judgment others have seen
Being the most talkative voice in every team meeting
items.explanation: Trust accumulates through observed track record.

items.prompt: A director consults an untitled engineer before infrastructure calls. Why?
choices: Company policy requires the director to do so
The engineer is secretly next in line to be promoted
That engineer's past judgment proved reliable
items.explanation: The director consults them because experience showed their calls are sound.

items.prompt: Is it a flaw that influence does not match titles?
choices: No, trust builds through repeated interaction
Yes, it proves the company is badly run
Yes, but only inside very large global companies
items.explanation: It is a natural consequence of how trust forms, not a defect.

items.prompt: Which of these can a title assign?
choices: Trust earned through past judgment
Authority to approve a request
A reputation for dependable advice
items.explanation: Titles assign formal authority. Trust and reputation have to be earned.

items.prompt: In a class, the student everyone asks about homework is...
choices: Automatically the class representative
Automatically named class representative for the whole term
Influential on that topic without any official role
items.explanation: Influence can sit in one topic with no role attached.

items.prompt: Where is someone's influence usually strongest?
choices: In the kind of decisions where their trust was earned
Across every type of decision made anywhere in the company
Only in the topic named by their job title
items.explanation: Influence is tied to a category of decisions.

items.prompt: Why can't an org chart encode influence?
choices: Chart tools cannot draw more than three levels
Trust is built through interaction, not assigned
Chart tools cannot draw more than three levels deep
items.explanation: A chart records assignments. Trust is not assigned.

items.prompt: Dana has no reports and no lead title. Priya sits two levels higher on paper, and the director asks her about staffing but never about infrastructure. An infrastructure proposal needs a champion. What does the evidence suggest?
choices: Priya's view must weigh more, since a higher placement on the chart always means more influence everywhere
Both views weigh the same, since influence is divided evenly by level
Dana's view likely weighs more on infrastructure, since influence belongs to a category of decisions
Neither view matters, since the proposal only needs a formal approver
items.explanation: Influence is tied to a category of decisions. The director consults Dana on infrastructure and Priya on staffing, so placement on the chart does not settle who weighs more here.
items.reference:
Authority vs. influence
authority: assigned by a title
influence: earned in one category of decisions
a person with no reports can still hold it
Why: trust is built through repeated interaction, so no chart can encode it.
items.learnMore:
Where influence comes from

A director trusts an infrastructure engineer because that engineer's calls kept proving right over years. That trust is specific to a category of decisions and it was never assigned by anyone.

Common mistake

Reading a missing title as missing weight.
items.reflection: Who in your life is trusted on one specific topic without having any official role there? How did that trust get built?

items.prompt: A director defers to one engineer on infrastructure after years of that engineer's calls proving right. How is that trust best described?
choices: Granted by title when the engineer joined, then slowly worn down
Earned through repeated demonstrated judgment, so no title could have assigned it
Granted by title when the engineer joined the team, then slowly worn down over the years
Inherited from the engineer's earlier manager when they moved teams
items.explanation: Trust comes from a track record seen over time. No title can assign it, and favors or inheritance are not how judgment-based trust forms.

items.prompt: A manager reasons: Sam has no authority, so Sam's opinion on releases cannot matter to the director. What does this get wrong?
choices: It treats authority as the only source of weight and ignores trust earned in a category
It assumes the director always overrules Sam's opinion on releases with their own preferred view
It forgets that authority is counted by the number of reports a person has
It confuses popularity with expertise, which a director always separates
items.explanation: The error is equating authority with weight. Trust earned in a category can give an untitled person real pull, and the other options attach unsupported claims to it.

The director transfers it to them the moment the budget lands
Their influence ends, since influence never survives decisions about money
Their design influence does not transfer automatically; budget trust may sit with someone else
items.explanation: Influence is earned per category of decision. Design trust says little about budget trust, so it does not transfer automatically.

items.prompt: Which of these is one of the four signals?
choices: Being named when a decision is explained
Having the largest and best-placed desk in the office
Sending the most messages each day
items.explanation: A decision is often explained by citing the person whose judgment mattered.

items.prompt: What does being looped in mean?
choices: Given formal authority over the whole topic area
Included in a conversation without owning it
Asked to chair the next meeting
items.explanation: Looped in means included although the topic is not theirs.

items.prompt: Chairing a meeting means...
choices: Writing the minutes for it
Skipping it on purpose
Officially leading it
items.explanation: The chair officially runs the meeting.

items.prompt: Someone's disagreement alone delays a decision. That is...
choices: A signal of real influence
A sign they dislike meetings
Proof they hold the top title
items.explanation: If one person's doubt can stall a call, their judgment carries weight.

items.prompt: A person is cc'd on threads they do not own. Does that count?
choices: No, people on the cc line never hold any influence
Yes, it is being looped in despite no formal role
Only if they reply within an hour
items.explanation: Being included without owning the topic is one of the signals.

items.prompt: Several signals point at the same person. What does that suggest?
choices: The signals must all be coincidence
That person holds the top title in the group
The informal network is becoming legible
items.explanation: Convergence on one person is hard to explain by chance.

items.prompt: A director says: Sam thought it made sense. Which signal is that?
choices: Sam is named as a reason for the decision
Sam was seated closest to the director's office
Sam sent the first message in the thread
items.explanation: Being cited when a decision is explained is a signal.

items.prompt: Someone attends every meeting but never speaks and never changes an outcome. Real influence?
choices: Yes, since presence is influence
No, that is only attendance
Yes, since they are invited so often
items.explanation: Attendance without any effect on outcomes shows nothing.

items.prompt: Over three weeks Rin, who has no lead title, is cc'd on every storage thread, is named by the lead as the reason a vendor was dropped, and once postponed a rollout by raising a doubt. What is the best reading?
choices: Rin shows three signals, so Rin likely holds real influence over storage decisions
Rin shows no signals, since a title is the only valid evidence of influence
Rin shows one signal, since being cc'd and being named are really the same
Rin is overreaching, since postponing a rollout by raising doubt proves a lack of influence
items.explanation: Rin shows being looped in, being named, and stalling a call by doubt. Three converging traces point to real influence over storage decisions regardless of title.
items.reference:
Four traces of real influence
looped in on threads without a formal role
named when a decision is explained
present across meetings but chairs none
disagreement alone stalls a decision
Why: the traces are observable, and several pointing at one person is what makes the network legible.
items.learnMore:
Reading traces, not titles

Influence is invisible on a chart but not in practice. Being cc'd, being cited, appearing everywhere without leading, and being able to stall a call each leave a trace you can see.

Common mistake

Counting plain attendance as a signal. Presence in the room is not the same as judgment shaping the room.
items.reflection: Pick a group you know well. Which of the four traces can you actually point to, and for whom?

A person invited to every planning meeting who never spoke or changed an outcome
items.explanation: Attendance with no effect on outcomes shows nothing. The other three observations each demonstrate judgment shaping a decision.

items.explanation: Any one trace may be innocent. When several land on one person, chance explains them poorly, and that convergence is what makes the network readable.

items.prompt: A manager is cc'd on everything because process requires copying the reporting chain. Does that cc count as a signal?
choices: Yes, since being cc'd always shows that a person is trusted
Not by itself, since the process forces the cc and reveals nobody's judgment
Yes, since the policy itself proves that the manager already holds informal influence
No, since managers can never hold informal influence at all
items.explanation: A cc required by process is not a choice anyone made about whom to consult, so it carries no information about influence. Managers can still hold informal influence, but this signal does not show it.

items.prompt: Besides who approved, what does the trace exercise record?
choices: Who attended the farewell lunch for the team
Who sent the first message of each working day
Who was actually consulted before the decision
items.explanation: The second column is the point: who was consulted first.

items.prompt: How many recent decisions does the exercise use?
choices: The last three significant ones
Every decision made this decade
Only the single biggest one
items.explanation: Three is enough to see whether a name repeats.

items.prompt: A name shows up in the consulted column across unrelated decisions. This is...
choices: A mistake made while taking the notes
The strongest signal of real influence
Proof that the person is the formal manager
items.explanation: Repetition across unrelated decisions shows a consistent pattern.

items.prompt: The exercise is mainly...
choices: A plan to befriend important people
A clever way to skip the formal approval steps
Diagnostic: a map of how decisions happen
items.explanation: It describes how decisions are made. It does not tell you whom to cultivate.

items.prompt: Could you run it in a school club?
choices: Yes, with any group that makes decisions
No, it only works inside very large companies
No, clubs never make real decisions
items.explanation: Any group that decides things has an informal network.

items.prompt: The column for who formally approved answers...
choices: Who people actually trusted first
Who had the official right to decide
Who disagreed with the final decision
items.explanation: Formal approval records the official right to decide.

items.prompt: Why use significant decisions rather than trivial ones?
choices: Trivial decisions are always kept secret
Significant decisions never have formal approvers
Real consultation happens when stakes are real
items.explanation: Nobody is consulted about trivia, so it shows nothing.

items.prompt: A name appears only once in the consulted column. Best read?
choices: Weak evidence; one case may be chance
Proof of very strong and lasting influence
Proof that the person holds no influence
items.explanation: A single case cannot show a pattern.

items.prompt: Trace: decision 1, approved by Director A, consulted Lee and Moss. Decision 2, approved by a VP, consulted Lee and Ortiz. Decision 3, approved by Director A, consulted Lee. Who is the strongest candidate for real influence?
choices: Director A, who formally approved two of the three decisions and so must have shaped them
Moss, who was consulted alongside Lee and so carries exactly equal weight
Ortiz, who was consulted on the one decision that the VP approved
Lee, who appears among those consulted in all three decisions with different approvers
items.explanation: Lee is consulted in all three decisions despite different approvers. A name repeating across unrelated decisions is the strongest signal. Approving formally is not the same as being consulted.
items.reference:
Trace the last three decisions
column 1: who formally approved
column 2: who was actually consulted first
a name repeating across unrelated decisions
= the strongest signal this exercise gives
Why: a consistent pattern of being checked before a call is not a one-off relationship.
items.learnMore:
Diagnosis, not guesswork

Instead of guessing who matters, write down real consultation for real decisions. One name in the consulted column across unrelated decisions beats any impression you had before.

Common mistake

Recording only who signed off, which reproduces the formal chart and hides the pattern.
items.reflection: Run the exercise mentally on three recent decisions in a group you belong to. Who shows up more than once?

items.prompt: You trace three recent decisions in your project group and Kai was consulted before each. What should you conclude?
choices: Kai is the formal leader and the official chart must be wrong
Kai should be befriended before any proposal even exists
Kai probably shapes how this group decides, so consider when your case should reach Kai
The trace is invalid, since consultation is informal and therefore cannot be observed by outsiders
items.explanation: Kai's repeated consultation suggests a real role in how this group decides. The map helps you plan when your case should reach Kai, which is not the same as befriending without a proposal.

It recorded the formal chain and missed the consulted column that reveals influence

It recorded consultation, which only measures how friendly people are
items.explanation: Recording only sign-offs reproduces the formal chart. The consulted column is where the informal pattern appears.

Keep it and count the approver as consulted so that every column looks full and complete
Stop the exercise, since two decisions can never show a pattern
Keep it and treat the empty column as proof nobody is influential
items.explanation: Routine decisions rarely involve consultation, so they hide the pattern. Replacing the weak case with a significant one keeps the exercise honest.

items.prompt: What is the map for?
choices: Avoiding anyone who must sign off on your work
Knowing where your case actually gets judged
Collecting favors from important people
items.explanation: Knowing where evaluation happens lets you get a fair hearing.

items.prompt: Which is a legitimate use of the map?
choices: Routing around people whose approval you owe
Flattering influential people regardless of whether the case has merit
Getting early feedback from people who shape the decision
items.explanation: Early feedback improves the proposal and surfaces objections.

items.prompt: Currying favor means...
choices: Winning someone over through flattery or favors
Winning approval through the strength of the case itself
Asking for feedback on a draft
items.explanation: It substitutes charm for substance.

items.prompt: After informal evaluation happens, the formal approval...
choices: Can safely be skipped now
Still has to be recorded
Is now officially void
items.explanation: The informal step adds to the formal one. It does not replace it.

items.prompt: The trace exercise is diagnostic. That means it...
choices: Ranks coworkers from most useful to least useful
Replaces the need for a good, sound proposal
Maps how decisions happen, not whom to befriend
items.explanation: It maps a process. It does not rank people.

items.prompt: What decides whether using the map is healthy?
choices: Whether the case is sound and the process respected
Whether the influencer ranks higher on the chart
Whether the conversation happens in private or openly
items.explanation: The same map serves honest and dishonest uses.

items.prompt: Asking an expert to review a design before you finalize it is...
choices: A way to dodge the formal approver
A legitimate use of the informal map
Currying favor with the powerful people
items.explanation: Seeking review on the substance is just good practice.

items.prompt: Mapping influence turns unhealthy when it becomes...
choices: A habit of noticing who tends to get consulted first
A way to learn how your org decides
A way to dodge those who should evaluate the work
items.explanation: The problem is avoiding evaluation, not noticing patterns.

items.prompt: Aisha and Ben both talk to the same influential person before formal approval. Aisha brings a sound proposal and asks them to find flaws. Ben brings a weak one hoping the endorsement will carry it. What separates them?
choices: Aisha uses the map to get merit a fair hearing; Ben substitutes access for merit
Aisha is networking and Ben is diagnosing, since only Ben applied the map to his proposal
Both act legitimately, since the identical conversation took place
Neither acts legitimately, since any informal talk bypasses the process
items.explanation: The conversation is the same, but Aisha invites scrutiny of a sound case while Ben tries to let access stand in for merit. What separates them is the strength of the case.
items.reference:
What the map is for
legit: early feedback from those who shape the call
legit: formal approval still happens afterwards
not this: favor-seeking regardless of merit
not this: routing around required approvers
Why: the same map serves both uses. The sound case and the respected process decide which one it is.
items.learnMore:
Access serves merit, not the reverse

Seeking review from the people who shape a decision improves a proposal and exposes objections early. Using the same access to avoid evaluation substitutes connection for substance.

Common mistake

Treating the map as a list of people to impress.
items.reflection: Think of a time you asked an expert for feedback before finishing something. How did that differ from seeking someone's approval?

items.prompt: After a trusted engineer backs a plan, a colleague says the director's sign-off can now be skipped. What is the flaw?
choices: Informal backing counts as the formal approval once it has been spoken aloud
The director's sign-off matters only for budgets and never for technical changes
Sign-off is a courtesy that the backer's word can replace if the backer ranks high enough on the chart
Informal backing adds to the formal approval and does not replace the official record
items.explanation: Informal evaluation happens before the official record, which still has to be made. The backer's word is not a substitute for the sign-off.

Yes, the influencer approved instead
No, the director still approved formally
items.explanation: Both paths ended at the same formal sign-off.

items.prompt: What did Path B add?
choices: A trusted evaluation before the formal step
A shortcut that goes around the formal approval step
A second competing formal chain
items.explanation: It added an upstream evaluation, not a bypass.

items.prompt: Why did Path A stall?
choices: The proposal contained a serious error
Nothing upstream vouched for it in the queue
The director refused to read any written proposals
items.explanation: It sat unevaluated among many similar requests.

items.prompt: What else improved Path B's proposal?
choices: The director rewrote the whole proposal text
A longer cover note was added
The influencer caught a real edge case
items.explanation: The informal review made the proposal better, not just faster.

items.prompt: A bottleneck is...
choices: A narrow point that slows everything else
A fast lane around the main queue
A person who approves most things instantly
items.explanation: A bottleneck is the narrow point in a flow.

items.prompt: Path A's bottleneck at the director was...
choices: Finding enough hours to read every proposal in the queue
Judging which request deserves careful attention
Finding time to write replies
items.explanation: The hard part was deciding what to evaluate deeply.

items.prompt: Vetted means...
choices: Approved by every department in the company
Rejected and then resubmitted
Reviewed by a trusted person beforehand
items.explanation: A vetted proposal has already passed someone's trusted review.

items.prompt: Path A's proposal was...
choices: Not wrong, only never evaluated
Rejected for being a weak proposal
Withdrawn by its author
items.explanation: It was never judged at all, which is different from being judged poor.

items.prompt: According to the comparison, what is the key difference between the two paths?
choices: Path B avoided the director's formal step entirely while Path A had to go through it
Path A was reviewed by a trusted person and Path B was not
Path B went through a longer formal chain with more approvers
Path B had a trusted evaluation upstream of the same formal step; Path A had none
items.explanation: Both paths ended at the same director and the same sign-off. The difference was a trusted evaluation placed before that step in Path B.
items.reference:
Same formal step, different upstream
Path A: formal chain only, no one vouches
Path B: trusted evaluation first, then the same director
Path B did not skip the director
Path B added a vetting step before the queue
Why: the gap was an upstream evaluation, not a missing process step.

Why the queue treated them differently

The director's real bottleneck is deciding which of many requests deserves careful attention. A proposal a trusted person already vetted answers that question. An unvetted one does not.

Common mistake

Concluding that Path B skipped the manager, when the director signed off in both paths.
items.reflection: Where in your own work does a request sit in a queue because nothing tells the reader it is worth their time?

items.prompt: A friend's request has sat in a queue for a month. Using this unit, what should they check first?

items.explanation: A stall can mean the request lacks vetting rather than that it was rejected. Checking for trusted review addresses the real bottleneck: deciding what deserves attention.

items.prompt: The trusted engineer leaves the company. Does loop in that person still work?
choices: Yes, the title stays attached to the role
Yes, the trust moves to the manager
No, the specific relationship is gone
items.explanation: The advice named a person, and that person is no longer there.

items.prompt: What part of the skill survives the departure?
choices: Observing who is consulted now
Remembering the old person's name
Copying the old chart exactly
items.explanation: The method of observing still works with new people.

items.prompt: The informal network is...
choices: A fixed map that new hires memorize early
A living structure that keeps changing
A document updated by HR
items.explanation: It changes as people join, leave and move.

items.prompt: How often should you re-run the trace?
choices: Once, during your first week on the team
Never, because the network does not really change
Periodically, as people join, leave and move
items.explanation: A one-time diagnosis goes stale.

Informal influence arrives automatically once you join
No proposal can ever be approved

The proposal itself, so it earns priority
The length of your cover note
items.explanation: Without informal vetting the proposal must stand on its own.

choices: Always valid in every company and team
Better than learning the method
Tied to a person and so it can expire
items.explanation: Person-specific advice ends when the person's role does.

choices: May be the new center of influence
Cannot hold any real influence over decisions
Replaces the formal chart

items.prompt: Six months on, the trusted engineer has moved to another organization. A new hire asks how to get an infrastructure proposal moving. What is the best answer?
choices: Keep looping in the departed engineer's old manager as a stand-in
Send it straight to the director, since the informal path has now closed for good
Observe who is consulted on infrastructure decisions now, and repeat the trace
Wait for the next published org chart before doing anything at all
items.explanation: The specific name is gone, but the method of observing who is consulted now still works. Stand-ins and waiting do not reproduce a trust relationship.

the skill survives: observe who is consulted now
